dietEvidence.body: Herbivory is inferred from the ceratopsian dentition and jaw apparatus. No gut contents are known, and the plants eaten are not preserved; the broad diet is a group-level inference.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A centrosaurine with a long nasal horn and several large spikes around the frill. The spikes are bone; their display function is inferred.
summary: A centrosaurine with a long nasal horn and several large spikes around the frill. The spikes are bone; their display function is inferred.

discovery.body: Named by Lambe, 1913. The holotype, CMN 344, is a skull from the Dinosaur Park Formation, Alberta. Several skulls and partial skeletons are known.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Several skulls and partial skeletons from Alberta.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Dinosaur Park Formation, Alberta records the species in the Late Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈77–75 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The nasal horn is tall, the frill bears long epiparietal spikes, and the body is robust.

behaviour.body: The nasal horn and frill spikes are preserved bone, but their function — display, species recognition or combat — is not demonstrated. Skull shape varies within the sample, and not every difference is taxonomic. No trackway or social group is known.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several skulls and partial skeletons from Alberta. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: Confidence is high for the skull and horn morphology. It is lower for horn and frill function, the growth series and social behaviour. No direct evidence of combat or herding is known.
